lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Here's a small trap in data analysis: you take the best value of every column and call it one result. But that row might never have existed.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It comes from a Python project called BatchBacktesting, from the AlgoETS group. Antoine read its source and wrote up what the code really does. The trap is in the analysis helper: grouping by instrument and taking the max. Each column's maximum is picked on its own, so one row can mix return, drawdown and duration from different runs.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the fix is to pick a real row first.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. Select the row by return, then talk about its drawdown. Antoine is clear that this is something he noticed reading code, not something he measured.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What does the engine actually do?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Think of a small data pipeline. You give it a list of instruments and a strategy. For each one it fetches prices, cleans them, runs a backtest, and writes results. It uses a thread pool, and the single-strategy runner defaults to four workers.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: No, and he says so. Those are code defaults, not measured throughput. Same for the assumptions: a hundred thousand in starting cash, a zero point two percent commission, exclusive orders. They live in the constructor, so they should sit next to any comparison of returns.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. Slippage, short availability, delisted stocks and corporate actions all need separate review. There's also an EMA strategy detail: it computes three moving averages, twenty, eighty and a hundred fifty, but entry decisions only compare the twenty and the eighty.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A failed instrument just returns nothing. If every instrument fails, the later step has no data to combine. And the multi-strategy helper nests thread pools inside a pool, so API rate limits deserve attention.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The takeaway is to read the assumptions, not just the charts.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. Antoine didn't rerun any simulation or make new return claims. The full write-up has the flowchart and links to the source files.
